prerequisiteEdges.justification: The laws are justified by counting repeated factors, which requires fluent translation between exponent and expanded form.
The identity n^0 = 1 is obtained by applying the quotient law to identical powers, so those laws must already be available.
Evaluating numerical examples of the laws after combining exponents requires reliable signed arithmetic.
Learners first need the criterion that distinguishes terminating expansions before they can consistently notate the complementary recurring cases.
Irrationals are recognised as neither terminating nor recurring, so those decimal types must already be distinguished.
Placing bounds such as 3.141 < π < 3.142 and comparing square-root estimates uses ordered comparison of signed decimals.

misconceptions.label: Minus always subtracts
misconceptions.description: Treats every minus sign as a binary subtraction and therefore miscomputes products or sums involving negative integers.

misconceptions.label: Exponent means multiply by the index
misconceptions.description: Evaluates a^n as a × n instead of n factors of a.

misconceptions.label: Add exponents across different bases
misconceptions.description: Writes a^m × b^n = (ab)^{m+n} or similar, combining exponents when bases differ.

misconceptions.label: Multiply exponents when multiplying powers
misconceptions.description: Applies a^m × a^n = a^{mn} instead of adding the exponents.

misconceptions.label: Any number to the power zero is zero
Short-looking decimals terminate
misconceptions.description: Judges termination from how many digits appear on a calculator rather than from the denominator’s primes.

misconceptions.label: Every non-terminating decimal is irrational
misconceptions.description: Classifies recurring decimals such as 0.333… as irrational because they do not stop.

misconceptions.label: π equals 22/7 exactly
misconceptions.description: Treats the familiar fraction 22/7 as the exact value of π rather than an approximation.

items.stem: Simplify 5^4 × 5^3, writing the result as a single power of 5.

options.rationale: The product-of-powers law adds the exponents when the bases are the same: 4 + 3 = 7.
Multiplies the exponents instead of adding them when multiplying powers of the same base.
Treats the product as if the bases were different and combines them while adding exponents.

items.keyRationale: Same base: add the exponents to obtain 5^7.

options.rationale: Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1, which follows from 8^n ÷ 8^n = 8^{n-n} = 8^0 = 1.
Assumes a number to the power zero is zero rather than one.
Leaves the base unchanged instead of applying the zero-exponent law.

items.keyRationale: n^0 = 1 for nonzero n, justified by subtracting equal exponents in a quotient of identical powers.

items.stem: The fraction 7/40 is in lowest terms. Does it have a terminating decimal expansion?

options.text: Yes, because 40 = 2^3 × 5 and the only primes in the denominator are 2 and 5.
options.rationale: A lowest-terms fraction terminates if and only if the denominator’s prime factors are only 2 and/or 5.

options.text: Yes, because a calculator shows 0.175, which looks short.
options.rationale: Judges termination from a short calculator display rather than the denominator’s primes.

options.text: No, because 40 is larger than 10 so the decimal cannot terminate.
options.rationale: Uses size of the denominator instead of its prime factors.

items.keyRationale: Denominator 40 factors as 2^3 × 5, so the decimal terminates.

items.stem: Which notation correctly represents the recurring decimal equal to 1/3?

options.rationale: 1/3 = 0.333… which is written with a bar over the repeating digit 3.

options.text: 0.3, which is irrational because it does not stop
options.rationale: Treats a recurring decimal as irrational simply because it does not terminate.

options.text: 0.33 with no repeat mark, because only two 3s appear
options.rationale: Confuses a truncated display with the infinite recurring expansion.

items.stem: On a number line, between which two consecutive integers does √10 lie?

options.rationale: 3^2 = 9 and 4^2 = 16, so √10 is a little more than 3 and less than 4.
Confuses √10 with π and treats 22/7 as an exact location.
Uses 2^2 = 4 instead of the squares that bound 10.

items.keyRationale: √10 is irrational and sits between 3 and 4 because 9 < 10 < 16.
